\chapter{Numbers 11–20 and Weather}
\label{ch:ml-numbers-and-weather}

This chapter is generated from the canonical micro-lessons used by Language Ladder.
Each section stays independently resumable and preserves the authored prerequisite order.

\section[\ml{പതിനൊന്ന്} — \ml{ഇരുപത്}]{\ml{പതിനൊന്ന്}, \ml{ഇരുപത്} — transparent "two-tens," matching Tamil closely}

\label{lesson:ML-C20-pathinonnu-irupathu}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Malayalam keeps the same "two-tens" idea you've now seen across this whole family — and here it's still fully visible on the surface, almost identically to its closest cousin, Tamil.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
Malayalam's teens echo \textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} (\emph{pathu}, "\textbf{ten}") plus each digit. \textbf{\ml{പതിനൊന്ന്}} (\emph{pathinonnu}) is 11, \textbf{\ml{പന്ത്രണ്ട്}} (\emph{panthraṇṭŭ}) is 12, and the pattern continues through \textbf{\ml{പത്തൊമ്പത്}} (\emph{pathompathu}, 19) — the same digit-plus-ten-echo compounding as its Dravidian cousins.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ഇരുപത്}} (\emph{irupathu}, "\textbf{twenty}") = \textbf{\ml{ഇരു}} (\emph{iru}, an older word for "\textbf{two}") + \textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} (\emph{pathu}, "\textbf{ten}") — still fully visible as "\textbf{two-tens}" today. This matches \textbf{Tamil's own} \emph{irupathu} almost letter-for-letter, both languages having kept this compound transparent — unlike Telugu's \emph{iravai}, which most likely continues the same underlying pattern but has worn down past the point of visibly splitting apart.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "pathinonnu, panthraṇṭŭ" — 11, 12{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "iru" — an older word for two, "pathu" — ten{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "irupathu" — twenty, "two-tens," transparent{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} How are Malayalam's teens built? (\textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} (ten) + a digit, compounded.) What two pieces build \textbf{\ml{ഇരുപത്}} (twenty)? (\textbf{\ml{ഇരു}} "two" + \textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} "ten" — "\textbf{two-tens}.") Which other Dravidian language keeps this exact same transparent compound for twenty? (\textbf{Tamil}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ}]{\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ} — "the state of time," an echo of Spanish's tiempo}

\label{lesson:ML-C20-kalavastha}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Remember Spanish's \emph{tiempo}, one word for both "time" and "weather"? Malayalam reaches the same connection between time and weather — but builds it as a compound instead of reusing one word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\textbf{\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ}} (\emph{kālāvastha}) = "\textbf{weather}" — built from:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{കാലം}} (\emph{kālam}, "\textbf{time}") — Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{काल}} (\emph{kāla}), "time," also the name of the god \textbf{Kāla} (an epithet of Śiva/Yama as the personification of time).
  \item \textbf{\ml{അവസ്ഥ}} (\emph{avastha}, "\textbf{state, condition}") — Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{अवस्था}} (\emph{avasthā}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{kālāvastha} literally means "\textbf{the state of time}" — a genuinely different construction than Spanish's \emph{tiempo}, but reaching for the exact same underlying idea: weather as bound up with time. Where Spanish just \textbf{reuses} its word for "time" to also mean "weather," Malayalam \textbf{compounds} "time" with "state" to build a brand-new word for the same concept.

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{മഴ} \ml{പെയ്യുന്നു}.} — "It's raining." — literally "\textbf{rain is falling}."
\end{quote}

(\emph{mazha peyyunnu.})
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "kālāvastha" — weather, "the state of time"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "kālam" — time, "avastha" — state{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "mazha peyyunnu" — it's raining, "rain is falling"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What are the two Sanskrit pieces of \textbf{\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ}}, and what does the whole word literally mean? (\textbf{\ml{കാലം}}, "time," + \textbf{\ml{അവസ്ഥ}}, "state" — "\textbf{the state of time}.") What earlier lesson does this echo, and how is the construction different? (\textbf{Spanish's \emph{tiempo}} — Spanish reuses ONE word for both senses; Malayalam \textbf{compounds} two separate words instead.) What word does Malayalam use for "rain"? (\textbf{\ml{മഴ}}, \emph{mazha}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
